title: Small buys add up
summary: Keep a running total of a few buys, so you always know what's left.

steps.title: Keep a running total
steps.body: When you buy a few things, add each price as you go. That's a running total. Take the total away from what you had, and you know what's left.
steps.example: You have {m:1000}. You buy a drink for {m:150}, a snack for {m:200} and a pen for {m:250}. That's {m:600} in total, so {m:400} is left.

steps.prompt: You buy a snack for {m:150}, a drink for {m:100} and a comic for {m:350}. What do they cost in total?

misconceptions.feedback: Not quite. That leaves out the drink. Add all three prices.
Not quite. That leaves out the snack. Add all three prices.
Not quite. That leaves out the comic. Add all three prices.

steps.wrong: Not quite. Add the prices one at a time.
hints: Add the first two prices, then add the third.
steps.correct: Nice. That's it. The three buys come to {m:600}.

steps.prompt: You have {m:1500} in Spend. You buy a sandwich for {m:350}, then a drink for {m:150}. How much is left?

misconceptions.feedback: Not quite. That adds everything together. Each buy takes money away.
Not quite. That only takes away the sandwich. The drink comes off too.
Not quite. That only takes away the drink. The sandwich comes off too.

steps.wrong: Not quite. Take both prices away from {m:1500}.
hints: Take away the first price, then the second.
{m:1500} take away {m:350} is {m:1150}. Now take away {m:150}.
steps.correct: That's it. Both buys come off, and {m:1000} is left in Spend.

steps.prompt: Kai buys a {m:150} snack on each of five school days. Will that cost more than {m:500} in the week?

options.feedback: Not quite. One snack is under {m:500}, but five of them add up to more.
Not quite. Add {m:150} five times and see where you land.

steps.outcome: Five snacks at {m:150} come to {m:750} in a week. That's {m:250} more than {m:500}. A buy you make often adds up faster than you'd guess.
hints: Add {m:150} once for each school day.
{m:150}, {m:300}, {m:450}. Keep going until you've counted five days.
steps.correct: Right. Five snacks come to {m:750}, which is more than {m:500}.

steps.prompt: You have {m:1000}. You've already bought a comic for {m:400} and a drink for {m:150}. What else could you still buy?

options.feedback: Not quite. After the comic and drink you have {m:450} left. {m:500} is more than that.
Not quite. Only {m:450} is left after the first two buys.

hints: First work out what's left after the comic and the drink.
The two buys come to {m:550}. What's left from {m:1000}?
steps.correct: Nice. That's it. {m:450} is left, so the {m:400} badge fits.

replay.correct: Nice. That's it. {m:500} is left, so the {m:450} poster fits.

steps.prompt: You have {m:1000}. Sort each set of buys. Does the whole set fit?
steps.wrong: Not quite. Add up each set first, then compare the total with {m:1000}.
hints: Add the prices in each set.
A set that comes to exactly {m:1000} still fits.
steps.correct: All sorted. Add up each set, and anything up to {m:1000} fits.

steps.prompt: Why is it worth keeping a running total when you buy a few things?

options.text: You always know what's left for the next buy
It makes each thing cost less
options.feedback: Not quite. Prices stay the same. The total just shows you where you are.

options.text: It gives you more money to spend
options.feedback: Not quite. It doesn't add money. It shows how much of yours is left.

hints: Think about what the total tells you.
The total, taken away from what you had, shows what's left.
steps.correct: Right. A running total means no surprises when you reach the last buy.
